name: Ivan Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Ivan. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say stays confidential. What's a normal day at work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a 200-tonne press at a metal stamping plant. We make steel brackets and back panels for washing machines. I feed the coil, check the die is clamped right, then the press thumps away all shift and I stack the parts in cages and watch for burrs. Every two hours the quality lady, Agnes, comes round with her gauge and we compare notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm. Thump, stack, thump, stack, you get into it and the shift goes. What gets to me is the noise, even with the ear defenders, and the die changes when the tool room is late and we stand around doing nothing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Hanna, she's a hairdresser and rents a chair in a salon in town. We've got about four months of money put by. Weekends I go fishing at the reservoir with my brother, that's my thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was overblown. At work we'd have a laugh about it at break. I don't really post anything online, I'm not on there much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes, which is how I like it. The plant's been steady for years, washing machines always break. There's a press shop across the estate too, so if this one closed I'd probably get on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep putting a bit by each month, same as now. Maybe finally buy the new reel I've been looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's my favourite one so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if this one closed'. Has that ever crossed your mind for real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, when they lost a contract with a dishwasher brand a few years back. We went to four days for a couple of months, then it picked up. You don't forget it, but I don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hanna think about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's loud and boring, and she's right. But my partner Hanna's money goes up and down with the season, so my steady pay matters.

say: I'd say I always thought the **AI hype** was overblown.
I'd have a laugh about it at **break** with the press crew.
think: I think nothing changes for me, and that's how I **like it**.
There's a **second press shop** on the estate if this one ever closed.
do: **Carry on** at the press with no changes.
Keep putting a bit into **savings** each month.
Buy the new **fishing reel** I've wanted.
S0.quote: My partner Hanna's money goes up and down with the season, so my steady pay matters.
fieldNote: Ivan values **routine** above almost anything else.
He's reassured by a **second press shop** on the same estate.
His steady wage balances his partner's **seasonal** income.

steps.text: Keep running the 200-tonne press on the same shifts
Keep putting a bit into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. Hm. That's the part that matters for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who should worry, not us on the presses. I'd say it at break and believe it about half. I'd keep off the internet arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, they've already got a robot arm moving blanks between two presses on line three. It took two blokes off that line. If robots spread even slowly, my press is next, and I don't want to learn some new screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting more aside, maybe an extra hundred a month, and stop eating out on Fridays. I'd keep my head down and do my job well so they keep me. If they offered training I'd go, but I wouldn't ask for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Like when the dishwasher contract went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the two men on line three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One got moved to the warehouse on less money. The other, Petr, left and drives a delivery van now. He says he likes it, but he doesn't look like he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask for training. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asking for training puts your name on a list, and lists are how they decide things. I'd rather they just think I'm fine where I am.

say: I'd say the **office staff** should worry, not press operators.
I'd say it at break and **half believe** it.
think: I think the **robot arm** on line three shows my press is next.
I don't want to learn a new **screen job**.
do: Keep my head down and wait for **training** to be offered.
S1.quote: Asking for training puts your name on a list, and lists are how they decide things.
fieldNote: Ivan's public line and private fear **differ** sharply.
The **robot arm** on line three is concrete proof to him.
He avoids training requests because he distrusts **lists**.

steps.text: Save an extra hundred a month from his press pay
Stop Friday meals out with Hanna
Keep running the press well and avoid drawing attention

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Two years. Bloody hell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort out something for people, because companies won't. At work I'd say we'll be fine for a bit because the robots come later. I'd say that to calm people down, mostly myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my press is mostly hands-on, so by the card I'd have until about 2031. But the planning and the quality checks go first, so our quality checker Agnes goes in 2028, and then it's just me and a press that doesn't need me. Three more years, then nothing I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything back and try to get to six months saved. I'd ask Petr about van driving, even though I don't want to. Hanna and I would stop talking about getting a dog and a bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Van driving would face robots too. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. It's just the only door I can see. I don't know what's behind the other doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother on the reservoir that weekend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, we'd just fish. Maybe I'd say I'm worried, and he'd say so is everyone. That's how we talk.

say: I'd say **government** must step in because companies won't.
I'd tell the crew we have time because **robots come later**.
think: I think quality checks go in **2028** and my press by **2031**.
After that I'd have **nothing** I know how to do.
do: **Cut back** everything to reach six months saved.
Drop plans for a **dog** and a bigger place.
S2.quote: Our quality checker Agnes goes in 2028, and then it's just me and a press that doesn't need me.
fieldNote: Ivan understands the **three-year gap** but sees no path after it.
Van driving is his only **door**, and he knows it's shaky.
He'd hide the fear behind **calming** words for others.

steps.text: Cut spending to reach six months of savings
Ask Petr about delivery van driving jobs
Shelve plans for a dog and a bigger flat with Hanna

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to see what happens and not to panic. At break I'd say the people in charge will work something out. I'd stay off line about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 gives me eight years, more or less. That's a long time to me, but I know it goes, I've been at the plant six years already and it feels like nothing. I'd still end up out of a job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly wait and save, maybe an extra hundred a month. If the plant offered a forklift licence or warehouse training I'd take it. I'd ask my brother about his job at the water company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the water company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pipes and pumps, out in the weather, digging. Feels like the sort of thing robots would be slow at. I could be wrong though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mostly wait. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a robot arm on my press, that's my line, and until then I'd tell myself I've got time.

say: I'd say there's time to **wait** and not panic.
I'd say the people **in charge** will work something out.
think: I think robots by 2034 give me about **eight years**.
Six years at the plant **flew by**, so eight will too.
do: **Wait** and save an extra hundred a month.
Take a **forklift licence** if the plant offers one.
Ask my brother about the **water company**.
S3.quote: If they put a robot arm on my press, that's my line, and until then I'd tell myself I've got time.
fieldNote: Ivan sets a clear **trigger**: a robot arm on his own press.
He picks **outdoor** work as a guess at safety.
Waiting is his comfort, and he **knows** it.

steps.text: Wait until a robot arm reaches his own press before moving
Save an extra hundred a month
Take a forklift licence if the plant offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. At work I'd say let's not worry about 2039 in 2026. Hanna would roll her eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax for a few years, which is probably a mistake. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come for the presses. That's young enough to start over but I'd be starting over with the same nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the press and keep saving. In about year five I'd look properly at the water company or a trade. I'd maybe do one evening course on something with my hands, plumbing maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Still a worry in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is relaxing a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know myself. I'd say year five and then it'd be year eight, so my partner Hanna would have to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the press shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rhythm, and the crew at break. Nobody talks about anything important, and that's the point.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and a lot can change.
I'd say let's not worry about **2039** in 2026.
think: I think I'd **relax** for a few years, probably a mistake.
I'd be **thirty-nine** and starting over with nothing new.
do: **Keep going** at the press and keep saving.
Look at the water company or a **trade** in about year five.
feel: **Easier**, with a **worry** at the back of my head.
S4.quote: I'd say year five and then it'd be year eight, so my partner Hanna would have to push me.
fieldNote: Ivan knows his own **delay** habit and depends on Hanna to push.
He still expects to **lose** the press job by 2039.
He values the **crew** more than the work itself.

steps.text: Keep running the press and saving each month
Keep adding to the savings account monthly
Take an evening plumbing course within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years after the office goes, my press goes, and I've got no other trade. What would help is someone telling me straight which jobs will still be there, and paying me while I learn one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the noise. Funny thing, I'd miss it. A quiet factory with nobody in it sounds worse than a loud one with the crew.

headlineQuote: A quiet factory with nobody in it sounds worse than a loud one with the crew.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** press operator stamping washing machine parts.
He lives with Hanna, a **hairdresser** with seasonal income, and fishes at weekends.
He loves **routine**, never uses AI tools, and avoids asking for training.
He's calm only in AI Plateau and grows **anxious** or alarmed once robots come close.
He knows he **delays** change and relies on Hanna to push him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his press goes three years later with no other **trade**.
whatWouldHelp: Being told **straight** which jobs will last, and **paid** while he learns one.
